newsitem.title: USA: GM to idle Windsor transmission plant Friday.
newsitem.headline: GM to idle Windsor transmission plant Friday.

text.p: General Motors Corp. said Tuesday it will suspend assembly operations at its Windsor transmission plant in Ontario on Friday because of a month-old strike in Oklahoma City, Okla.

The plant, which makes four-speed automatic transmissions for front-wheel drive cars, is the latest facility affected by strikes by the United Auto Workers union that have besieged U.S. automakers since early April.

Assembly at the Windsor plant will resume on Monday, GM Canada spokesman Greg Gibson said. About 250 members of the Canadian Auto Worker Local 1973 who work on two shifts will be idled. The plant employs a total of 1,500 hourly workers.
About 28,200 union workers at GM and Chrysler Corp. are either on strike or idled because of labour disputes at three plants in the United States.

As of Tuesday, GM and Chrysler have lost production of 119,122 units, many of those high-profit sport/utility vehicles and pickup trucks, according to Michael Robinet, managing director of CSM Forecasting Inc., a consultant in Farmington Hills, Mich.
Analysts estimated last week the Chrysler strike alone had cost the nation's third-largest automaker $300 million -- a figure that is growing $15 million to $20 million a day.

Union and company representatives Tuesday reported slight progress on resolving the strikes. At the Oklahoma City car plant, where 3,500 UAW members walked off the job April 4, a union spokeswoman said bargainers have resolved some minor issues and have moved on to more major concerns.
"They're talking about all the big issues, even though I still feel they could take a while," said Yvonne Smith, vice president of UAW Local 1999.
Workers at the plant, who have not signed a new local contract, want GM to restore some of the 900 jobs the automaker cut when it launched the new Malibu and Cutlass late last year.

Analysts estimate GM lost several thousand Malibu sales in April because of the strike. GM has suspended nearly all its advertising on the car, a crucial part of its plans to regain market share in the key mid-size car segment.

At the other GM strike, in Pontiac, Mich., a spokesman for UAW Local 594 said negotiators have made little headway in addressing the major outsourcing and staffing issues at the centre of that dispute.
"It's very, very slow, very slow," said the spokesman, who would not give his name.

About 5,850 members of Local 594 struck GM's Pontiac East full-size pickup truck assembly plant and related facilities on April 22. The plant typically makes about 6,000 of the popular extended cab pickup models a week. Union members want GM to address health and safety issues and add up to 600 jobs.
Analysts estimate the Pontiac strike is costing GM $4.5 million to $5 million a day, while the Oklahoma City walkout is costing less.

Chrysler spokesman Tony Cervone said senior level talks between Thomas Gallagher, the company's vice president of employee relations, and Jack Laskowski, head of the UAW's Chrysler department, continue intermittently. Talks are occurring both on the phone and in person, he said.

A strike April 9 by 1,856 UAW members at Chrysler's Mound Road Engine plant in Detroit has forced the company to suspend operations at eight assembly operations in North America. The number of workers affected is 18,916, down from more than 22,000 last week because the company has called employees back to work at parts plants in Kokomo, Ind., and Kenosha, Wis.
